rationale: Most formations still preserve only sparse species-to-species intermediates, and palaeontologists routinely name successive morphs in one formation as separate chronospecies. Denser records in a minority of lineages show that 'only a few' links is not universal.

First appearances are biased young by incomplete sampling, and earlier fossils of many groups continue to turn up, often far from the region of their apparent debut. Some radiations are genuinely rapid, so sudden origins are not always pure artefacts.

Key innovations such as flight, endothermy, or a fully aquatic habit are often followed by geologically rapid diversification and wide geographic spread. The long preceding evolution of the novelty itself is also a common pattern.

The interval of life before the oldest Cambrian–Silurian animal faunas is far longer than the time since, and the oceans were already full of microbial life. Abundant complex animals do not occupy most of that earlier span, so 'swarmed with living creatures' holds mainly for microbes.

Continents have collided, split, and changed latitude repeatedly since the early Palaeozoic, and ocean basins have opened and closed. The absence of old sediments on oceanic islands reflects recycling of ocean crust, not fixed positions of oceans and continents.

Many lineages add species one after another, especially in well-sampled Cenozoic sections. Radiations and post-extinction recoveries also produce geologically clustered batches, so a rule of very slow successive appearance rather than batches does not hold.

Rates and amounts of morphological and taxonomic change differ sharply among clades, from near-static 'living fossil' lineages to rapidly evolving ones. Equal rates across genera and classes are not observed.

Terrestrial species, especially vertebrates, often have shorter durations and faster morphological turnover than many marine invertebrate groups. The contrast is a tendency with many exceptions, not a clean land-versus-sea rule.

Once a lineage is truly extinct, the same species does not re-evolve, because a later form has a different history. Convergence can restore a similar appearance, and sampling gaps can mimic reappearance, but identical return is not observed.

A clade that still has members persists through an unbroken chain of generations and does not re-evolve after true extinction. In the fossil record, genera and families often vanish and later reappear because of sampling gaps, so continuity of occurrence is not what the rocks show.

Many genera and families increase in richness and later decline, a common unimodal trajectory. Rises and falls are often abrupt—radiations and mass extinctions—so a general rule of gradual increase to a maximum and gradual decrease is only partly right.

Background extinction frequently proceeds by range contraction, region by region. Global mass extinctions also remove many species and whole groups together, so catastrophes are a real mode of disappearance, not a discarded alternative.

Some clades radiate quickly and then dwindle over a longer interval, and sudden endings such as the ammonites are correctly noted as exceptions. Many other groups are truncated by mass extinctions faster than they arose, so slower extinction is not a reliable general rule.

Range contraction and falling abundance commonly precede species extinction in both the fossil record and historically documented losses. Abrupt kills at mass extinctions supply exceptions, but the usual sequence is rarity first.

Over long spans, origination and extinction are often similar in magnitude, so richness does not grow without limit. Diversity has still risen through later geological time in many compilations, and new species do not by themselves cause an equal number of extinctions.

Competition is often stronger among close relatives, and character displacement is real. Parent species commonly survive budding speciation, and congeners routinely coexist, so descendants do not generally exterminate the parent and its nearest allies.

Major turnovers in marine faunas are correlated worldwide well enough that distant formations are matched by their fossils. First and last appearances are often somewhat diachronous, but in a broad geological sense the changes are nearly synchronous.

On average, older fossils are more distant in form and relationship from living species, as expected from divergence through time. Living fossils and long static lineages are real exceptions to the general rule.

Extinct forms often occupy morphological and phylogenetic positions between living groups and fit with them in one tree of life. Many fossils are side branches or members of wholly extinct clades rather than gap-fillers between living genera, families, and orders.

Early members of lineages that later diverged strongly tend to share more characters than their living descendants do, as with early stem groups of vertebrates and arthropods. The approach is often slight, and convergence or incomplete fossils can obscure it.

Successive formations share far more taxa and morphologies than formations far apart in time, which is why faunal succession can be ordered. Each interval's biota is broadly intermediate, with sharper breaks at mass extinctions.

Later biotas are not known to be generally superior competitors to earlier ones under a similar climate; incumbency and local adaptation often favour established forms. Arms-race escalation occurs in some predator–prey systems, but it does not establish that recent faunas would routinely exterminate older ones.

Late Cenozoic fossils on a continent are typically closest to that continent's living fauna, as with Australian marsupials and South American xenarthrans. Interchange and regional extinction add outsiders, but the regional succession of types is a robust pattern.

Climatically similar regions, such as the Mediterranean-climate zones of Australia, southern Africa, and western South America, have profoundly different floras and faunas. Climate shapes life form and filters who can live somewhere, but it does not account for the taxonomic similarities and differences among regions.

Oceans, mountain chains, deserts, and deep-water straits coincide with major biotic breaks, and older, harder barriers generally bound greater differences. Large rivers are weaker barriers than Darwin's list implies, but the overall correspondence is strong.

Within a continent or ocean basin, species that replace one another geographically or by habitat are usually relatives, not ecological analogues drawn from other regions. Phylogenies repeatedly recover this provincial affinity.

Shared ancestry explains why living and extinct inhabitants of a region resemble one another beyond what climate requires. Regional differences are produced mainly by divergent evolution under selection, with direct environmental moulding of heredity only a minor factor; drift and dispersal history also contribute.

Moving together into a new country does not freeze a biota: new climates, genetic drift, and isolation regularly modify colonists. Biotic interactions matter, but isolation and abiotic novelty themselves cause substantial change.

Endemism is common at family level and becomes the norm toward genera and sections, and tightly knit genera are usually geographically restricted. Some natural genera are widespread, so the second clause is a strong tendency rather than a rule without exceptions.

A species originates in one population and then spreads as far as dispersal and suitable conditions allow. Repeated independent origins occur in some polyploid plants, so single origin is the usual case rather than an exceptionless law.

True oceanic islands were not tied to continents by continuous land during the lifetime of living species, and the broad land-bridge schemes of the period are rejected. Intermittent connections such as Beringia did join some continents, so a blanket denial of recent continental union is too strong.

A minority of seeds can float in seawater and still germinate, and ocean crossings of several hundred miles are documented. The specific tenth of a flora and the 900-mile figure come from limited trials and vary widely among floras, so they are only a rough order of magnitude.

Currents, birds, and rafts readily move organisms across a few hundred miles, and distant continental floras do stay largely distinct. The same occasional means also cross oceans between distant continents often enough that a flat prohibition is false.

Shared arctic–alpine species on separated mountains of Europe and North America are largely populations that spread in cold intervals and retreated as climate warmed. Some survived in separate refugia with deeper splits, but the glacial-relict account is the main explanation.

Temperate North America and Europe share many allied but few identical forms because of earlier Holarctic connections and southward retreat. Those links were broader and often older than a warm Pliocene circumpolar belt alone, with Asia and North Atlantic routes both important.

The last glacial maximum cooled both hemispheres and the tropics at the same time, and the glacial interval was long at a given place. Millennial swings are not perfectly in phase between the poles, so worldwide simultaneity is only partial.

Northern temperate and arctic–alpine plants are often identical or closely allied, and a few lineages are shared with southern temperate and tropical mountains. Tropical alpine floras are frequently derived from local tropical ancestors, so a worldwide close relationship of all these floras does not hold.

More plant lineages moved from north to south than the reverse, and the larger northern landmass and species pool help explain the asymmetry. Treating northern forms as more advanced or competitively perfected is not supported.

European plants and animals have naturalised in large numbers in the Río de la Plata region and, to a lesser extent, Australia, and have displaced some natives. Far fewer southern-hemisphere species have naturalised in Europe, though human trade patterns contribute to the asymmetry.

Antarctica was vegetated in warmer pre-glacial times and is central to many southern-hemisphere disjunctions now linking South America, Australia, and New Zealand. Those links were mainly ancient land connections as the southern continents separated, with occasional overseas transport a secondary route.

Many freshwater plants, insects, molluscs, and small crustaceans have enormous ranges despite land and sea barriers, and related species recur worldwide. The pattern is a real tendency, not a description of every freshwater group.

Strictly freshwater fish species are almost never naturally shared by distant continents, while within a continent river systems share species in an irregular patchwork. Salt-tolerant fishes and a few natural exceptions keep the 'never' from being absolute.

Waterbirds carry seeds, resting eggs, and other propagules between isolated waters and are a primary reason many freshwater plants and small animals are so widespread. Other vectors exist, but bird transport is the main one for this scope.

Oceanic islands hold far fewer species than continental areas of the same size across plants and animals. Isolation and limited colonisation, not a systematically harsher physical setting, account for the impoverishment.

Remote islands often have very high endemism relative to their area, as in the Galápagos, Hawaii, and many smaller oceanic islands. That matches modification of occasional colonists after they arrive in isolation.

On a given island, groups that arrive easily and repeatedly, such as seabirds and many marine shells, show much less endemism than poor dispersers. Continued gene flow as well as undisturbed biotic relations explains the limited modification.

Woodiness has evolved repeatedly in herbaceous plant lineages on oceanic islands, producing shrubs and trees in groups that are herbaceous on continents. Release from continental trees and selection for stature are the leading explanation, alongside longer life cycles.

Most remote oceanic islands lack native frogs, toads, and salamanders, introduced amphibians often thrive, and salt water kills them and their eggs. Native frogs on some oceanic islands, such as Fiji, show that the absence is a strong rule with exceptions.

Terrestrial mammals are genuinely poor ocean dispersers, and small mammals often flourish after introduction. Native rodents on the Galápagos, more than 300 miles from a continent, and a few other rafting cases falsify the absolute absence claim.

Bats reach most oceanic islands that can support them and have produced endemic species on remote archipelagos, consistent with flight followed by local modification. Some small or harsh islands have no bats, so 'almost every island' is a little strong.

Shelf islands separated by shallow water share mainland mammals or close allies because they were connected at low sea level, whereas deep-water gaps coincide with distinct species and genera. Depth predicts affinity beyond distance alone.

Island endemics are almost always allied to the nearest continent or neighbouring islands, as with Galápagos biotas to the Americas and Cape Verde biotas to Africa, even when climates resemble a more distant region. Long-distance exceptions exist but do not overturn the rule.

Endemics on the islands of one archipelago are usually one another's closest relatives, because they share a source or spread between islands, as in Galápagos finches and Hawaiian radiations. Multiple independent colonisations sometimes make a mainland species the nearer relative.

Introduced species are sometimes distant relatives of the natives they join, which fits stronger competition among close kin. Tests of this pattern are mixed, and many naturalised species belong to genera already present, so it is not a general rule.

Island, mountain, lake, and cave biotas, when not shared outright with a source, are typically modified relatives of the nearest accessible region and are adapted to the new setting. Unexpected long-distance colonists occur, but the accessible-source rule is the usual case.

Regions that share many representative species often also share some identical species and a trail of doubtful forms, consistent with past connection or migration. Fully speciated disjunctions, such as parts of the eastern Asian and eastern North American floras, can lack shared species.

Very small organisms with tiny propagules, including many microbes, bryophytes, and small invertebrates, tend to range more widely than large animals. 'Lower in the scale' is not a coherent axis, and slower change is not a reliable cause.

Closer relatives are generally nearer in age and geography, because they share a recent ancestor in a particular place. Relicts, long-distance dispersal, and living fossils whose nearest kin are ancient supply frequent exceptions.

Nested groups within groups are the expected shape of a tree in which descendants of one ancestor diverge and extinction removes intermediates. That is the standard explanation of the taxonomic hierarchy.

A natural classification tracks closeness of descent, and phylogeny is what the hierarchy expresses. Descent is not the only cause of similarity: convergence also produces resemblances that classification must set aside.

Characters that stay constant across many species, often those less tied to a particular habit, carry more weight in higher classification. Some adaptive traits are conserved after a single origin, and neutral characters also classify well, so the link is general rather than strict.

Ranks above species have no objective threshold; orders, families, and genera are conventional and are often raised or lowered as more relatives are found. Genealogy can be real while the rank labels remain almost arbitrary.

A natural arrangement has to follow genealogy, and sister branches routinely differ enormously in how much they have changed. Expressing that disparity by different ranks matches traditional practice, though rank itself is not fixed by the amount of change.

Breeds and natural varieties nest into groups under groups for the same reason species do: shared descent plus unequal amounts of modification. Domestic animals such as pigeons and dogs show the hierarchy plainly.

A trait shared by many species that live in very different ways is usually inherited from a common ancestor, which is why it, and likewise rudimentary structures, ranks highly in classification. Developmental constraint can preserve a trait without that being the usual explanation.

Distinct lineages often converge in external form under similar conditions, and those analogies obscure relationship between groups while the same traits can mark true affinity inside one group. Classic cases include marine mammals and fishes, and succulent plants of separate families.

Life falls into relatively few large clades because of common ancestry and because extinction has pruned many early branches. Large groups do not reliably keep expanding and replacing smaller ones; dominant clades also die out and small ones later radiate.

Phylogenetically isolated groups such as ginkgoes, coelacanths, and tuatara are typically species-poor remnants of formerly broader clades, and their few species are markedly distinct. Some species-poor groups are young or narrowly adapted rather than survivors of heavy extinction.

When one group shows a genuine affinity to another, the link is usually to the group as a whole through characters of a shared ancestor, not to one living species. Living species are rarely the ancestors of other groups.

Extinction of intermediate forms widens the gaps between surviving groups. Birds are separated from other living vertebrates by the loss of many stem forms, a gap the fossil record has steadily filled.

Within a class, homologous parts change enormously in size and shape while their order of connection is conserved; limb bones are not transposed. Elements can be lost, fused, or multiplied, but the sequence itself is remarkably stable.

The common pattern of organs within a class is inheritance from an ancestor that already had that layout, later altered in small steps for different functions without rearranging the parts. Mammal limbs and insect mouthparts fit this account.

Serial organs in arthropods and the leaf-like nature of floral parts reflect ancestors with many repeated parts later specialised for different roles. The skull is not a row of transformed vertebrae, so that classic example of the same principle is wrong.

Embryos of different members of a class are often more alike than the adults, and many shared traits are not adaptations to embryonic life. The earliest stages can diverge, with the strongest resemblance at a mid-embryonic stage, so the similarity is common rather than uniform.

Free-living larvae are under selection and are as functionally fitted to their own lives as adults are, and allied species can differ more as larvae than as adults. Most larvae nevertheless retain the broader embryonic resemblances of their class.
